Senses.Explanation: Wuyi Yuanlai supplies the clearest corpus definition: there are two awakenings, “interpretive awakening obtained from written words and speech” and “thorough awakening obtained by investigating on one’s own part”; he adds, “interpretive awakening is like hearing someone describe a thing; thorough awakening is like seeing the thing with one’s own eyes” (解悟者如聞人說物，徹悟者如親眼見物). Other records say not to stop if one has not thoroughly awakened, describe the World-honored One seeing the morning star and thoroughly awakening, and contrast the many who thoroughly awaken with the equally many who misunderstand. Thus the Chan record bends an ordinary intensive verb into a named contrast with “interpretive awakening” (解悟), while also using it in lineage biographies; the direct contrast, not an imported theory of enlightenment, controls the gloss.

Senses.Explanation: The monastery abbot's room or institutional quarters. The term occurs 5,717 times in 391 allowed texts. 'Enter the abbot's quarters' (入方丈) occurs 468 times, while 'return to the abbot's quarters' (歸方丈) occurs 2,176 times. Xinzhou Zhichang reports going alone at midnight 'into the abbot's quarters to bow and make an earnest request' (入方丈禮拜哀請). Mazu Daoyi returns to the quarters and Layman Pang follows him (師歸方丈。居士隨後). Linji Yixuan's record has an unnamed head monk follow Linji up to the quarters and bow. Chuiwan Guangzhen supplies an explicit naming contrast: 'the ancients called it the abbot's ground; this old monk calls it the abbot's room' (古人喚作方丈地，老僧喚作方丈室). Zen bends the room into a repeated destination for direct exchange and a named institutional interior.

Senses.Explanation: By metonymy, the room names its resident: the monastery's abbot or abbot-monk. The Chan Grove Admonitions speaks of 'those today who occupy the abbot's quarters' (今之踞方丈者) while criticizing what those residents take from the community. Later records use the explicit compound 'abbot-monk' (方丈和尚) and tell hearers that they must 'ask the abbot-monk' (請問方丈和尚). The same personal use appears when Xueguan Zhiyin presents a verse to the abbot. English 'the abbot' is warranted when the syntax denotes the resident person rather than movement into a room; the stored evidence does not require a separate abstract-abbacy target.
